Don’t Skip the Baseline:
A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic
Expert Skipping in MoEs

Jakob Steimle Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Tensordyne    Thomas Elsken Affiliation: Tensordyne    Daniel Ehrhardt Affiliation: Tensordyne    Lukas Rinder  Daniel Cremers  Xi Wang Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Tensordyne Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Ulm UniversityCorrespondence: jakob.steimle@tensordyne.ai
Abstract

A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts kk (i.e., same reduced kk across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective kk achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective kk in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static kk reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.

1 Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become one of the leading paradigms for model architectures, activating only a small subset of all parameters (called “experts”) during each forward pass. Typical models (Yang et al., 2025a; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Gemma Team et al., 2026) activate k=8k=8 out of 128 to 512 available experts—fixed across all layers and tokens. Some methods for selecting a reduced number of experts already during (pre)training have been proposed (Raposo et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), however these approaches are not yet adopted in major open-weight model families. We therefore focus on the question: given a trained model, can we reduce the active number of experts while preserving quality by reducing this kk during inference, potentially dynamically per token and/or per layer?

Static, fixed-kk MoE inference has clear practical advantages: it is simple to implement, requires no additional calibration (i.e., selecting kk given an input token and layer), and, most importantly, matches the routing behavior learned during training. It further produces predictable, uniform compute and memory-access patterns across tokens. However, research has shown that not every token requires the same number of experts (Lu et al., 2024). As a result, different approaches have been proposed to optimize inference costs by varying kk. These approaches include static pruning, which permanently reduces the set of available experts to conserve memory, and (dynamic) skipping, which instead varies the number of active experts per token at inference time. Yang et al. (2025b) describe three benefits dynamic skipping can offer over fixed-kk inference: first, it reduces the total number of computations performed during each forward pass. Second, in small-batch scenarios, it reduces the number of unique experts active, lowering memory bandwidth requirements. Third, in a distributed deployment scenario, it can reduce communication overhead and improve load balancing.

Some recent methods have considered dynamic expert skipping as an add-on to static model pruning, rather than evaluating its benefits on its own, making it difficult to disentangle how much of the reported benefit comes from skipping itself versus the accompanying pruning. Beyond that, the proposed methods have become increasingly complex and costly. These range from calibrated scores (Lu et al., 2024) to similarity approaches (Bai et al., 2025b), and learned allocators (Yue et al., 2025). One of the most recent approaches by Huang et al. (2026) is MoDES, which uses calibrated modality-aware thresholds and reports near original performance while reducing the number of active experts by over 80%80\%. The combination of different calibration regimes, operating points (method configurations), and evaluations makes comparison difficult. To close this gap, this study aims to provide a fair comparison across methods, benchmarks and inference-compute budget.

Our contributions:

  1. 1.

    A unified taxonomy of dynamic expert-skipping strategies, organized by the signal they add over the standard MoE router (Table 1).

  2. 2.

    A controlled, matched expert compute comparison of four representative methods against a static top-kk baseline across different modalities and models, made fair by measuring compute at test time and comparing the full quality-compute frontier.

  3. 3.

    A zero-calibration, per-modality static top-kk configuration (kvision=1k_{\text{vision}}=1–22, ktext=6k_{\text{text}}=6) that recovers ≈95%\approx 95\% of original quality at ≈85%\approx 85\% fewer active experts in vision-heavy tasks.

  4. 4.

    The insight that, despite their added complexity and cost, contemporary dynamic skipping methods do not systematically outperform a simple static baseline at matched compute.

We find that, across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings, the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently and by large margins. To allow reproducibility we will release our code, including (re-)implementations of all evaluated skipping methods. This further allows the original authors to verify our implementations.

2 Background

A number of methods have been proposed to leverage the different expert needs of tokens. We distinguish between expert skipping, which reduces the set of experts activated per token, and expert rerouting, which selects different experts than those chosen by the router.

Expert Skipping

methods target existing static top-kk models. An early such strategy, “Not all Experts are Equal” (NAEE) (Lu et al., 2024), skips a tail expert whenever its routing score falls short of the top expert’s by a calibrated margin; Bai et al. (2025b) extend this criterion with an inter-expert redundancy term. Further criteria include per-token sensitivity (Zhong et al., 2024), confidence-triggered re-evaluation with the full expert set (Zhao et al., 2025), and data-free per-layer expert budgets (Chitty-Venkata et al., 2025). Huang et al. (2026) extend threshold-based skipping to the multimodal domain with per-layer importance scores and per-modality thresholds, while Yue et al. (2025) train a per-token classifier via reinforcement learning to predict the required expert count.

Expert Rerouting

methods alter which experts are selected rather than how many, steering tokens toward cached or already-active experts to reduce weight-loading overhead (Skliar et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Oncescu et al., 2025). Their benefit hinges on shrinking the unique set of active experts per forward pass. This reduces overhead due to memory bandwidth, but only works in small batch sizes. At sufficiently large batch sizes nearly all experts are required.

For this paper we focus on dynamic skipping, as rerouting offers limited benefit in common (large batch) inference scenarios. We explicitly study skipping in isolation from the pruning stages that some of these methods originally include. As skipping is orthogonal and composable with any pruning method, this lets us attribute quality differences to the skipping decision itself. Closest to our baseline (next section), Xia et al. (2025) reduce the expert count for vision tokens to a fixed kvision<kk_{\text{vision}}<k from a chosen onset layer onward, while text tokens always retain the full kk; they ablate (kvisionk_{\text{vision}}, onset layer) at moderate reductions (kvision=4k_{\text{vision}}=4–55 of 88) and deploy the mechanism jointly with visual token pruning.

3 Methodology

3.1 Baselines

Our natural baseline for expert skipping methods builds on the model’s native routing: statically reducing the number of experts kk. We refer to this baseline as softmax top-kk, based on the selection criteria. As a reminder, for popular mixture of expert models like Qwen3, the router generates logits, which are normalized with softmax before the top-kk experts are selected. We expand on this approach for multimodal models by defining separate kk values for each modality: ktextk_{\text{text}} and kvisionk_{\text{vision}}. This separate treatment of modalities is inspired by prior work (Huang et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2025). For models that support image and video tokens separately, we use kvisionk_{\text{vision}} for both token types. Both baseline variants share the same benefit: they are calibration-free and static.

3.2 Methods for comparison

We evaluate four representative dynamic skipping methods: NAEE (Lu et al., 2024), DiEP (Bai et al., 2025b), MoDES (Huang et al., 2026), and Ada-K (Yue et al., 2025), summarized in Table 1. We describe them based on a number of concrete properties of the methods: their criteria, decision rule, calibration phase and tunable parameters. We further discuss the calibration time necessary for a single operating point. Both NAEE and DiEP also provide methods for expert pruning that they combine with the skipping approach. We only consider the dynamic skipping approach here.

Skipping Criteria

The first major differentiating factor between the methods is the skipping criteria. While our baselines and NAEE skip experts based entirely on the routing scores (also called gate weights), the other methods expand on this: DiEP uses an inter-expert Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) (Kornblith et al., 2019) statistic that measures redundancy in individual experts, while MoDES adds a global layer importance factor. Ada-K is different here, as it uses the hidden state of the token rather than the routing scores as a criteria.

Decision Rule

Our baselines have the simplest rules, as they retain the top-kk experts and vary only the kk. NAEE on the other hand uses the cumulative routing scores and compares their ratio against a calibrated threshold. DiEP and MoDES adapt the concept from NAEE with a more complex threshold and score. All methods except for DiEP always keep the expert order intact. Further, all dynamic methods except for MoDES will always retain at least the first selected expert. Ada-K differs from the other methods in its decision rule: rather than deciding whether a given expert should be skipped, it instead predicts the number of experts that should be retained using what they call an Allocator.

Calibration

While our baselines are calibration free, NAEE, DiEP and MoDES all require calibration. NAEE calibrates the threshold value used for skipping, while DiEP calibrates this (γ1\gamma_{1}) as well as the CKA similarity metric between experts (γ2​(e0,ei)\gamma_{2}(e_{0},e_{i})). MoDES first calibrates the importance α(l)\alpha^{(l)} of each layer and then identifies the ideal thresholds (τv,t\tau_{v,t}) needed to achieve a target skipping ratio. Ada-K uses a unique approach, as it optimizes the linear layer of the Allocator using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), a type of reinforcement learning.

Tunable Parameters

Tunable parameters can be adjusted to vary the targeted operating point. For NAEE this comes in the form of the β\beta quantile. When calibrating, the cumulative ratio between the routing scores is collected for each layer. By selecting an appropriate quantile we can sweep across operating points, skipping more or less experts. NAEE natively uses only the median. For DiEP we again sweep the quantile for the skipping parameter γ1\gamma_{1}, in their paper they primarily use the median as an operating point. For MoDES the tunable parameter is the target skip ratio, as part of their calibration procedure they find the ideal thresholds (τv,t\tau_{v,t}) that achieve the target skip ratio. Lastly Ada-K has one main parameter λ\lambda. This defines the cost of adding additional experts in the strategy. A higher cost λ\lambda results in fewer experts being predicted to be needed.

Calibration Cost

We calculate the calibration cost using the original code release for MoDES and use our own implementation for the other methods on a single A100 80GB. While our static baselines are free, since they are calibration free, the advanced dynamic skipping methods have significantly different requirements. DiEP and NAEE are both relatively fast to compute, requiring approximately half an hour to calibrate for Qwen3-30B-A3B, depending on calibration data. Ada-K also varies significantly, but uses a much larger training dataset, resulting in around 2.5 hours of training time. MoDES requires the longest calibration at nearly 20 hours, as both the layer importance score measurement and the frontier search involve many forward passes through the full model.

We selected these methods as representative: they are current and use significantly different approaches to skipping. DiEP with its consideration of expert redundancy, Ada-K with its training approach, MoDES due to the multimodality and NAEE as the simplest calibration-based approach all reflect distinct criteria for selecting experts that can be skipped.

3.3 Quantifying Per-Token Expert Effort

All considered skipping strategies activate fewer experts for some tokens. To compare these savings on a common, hardware-agnostic axis, we define effective K (KeffK_{\text{eff}}) as a proxy metric. KeffK_{\text{eff}} is the mean number of routed experts per token, averaged across all tokens and layers: Keff=1T⋅L​∑t=1T∑l=1Lkt,lK_{\text{eff}}\;=\;\frac{1}{T\cdot L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{l=1}^{L}k_{t,l}, where kt,lk_{t,l} is the number of experts activated for token tt in layer ll. For the static softmax top-kk baseline, Keff=kK_{\text{eff}}=k by construction, whereas for the dynamic strategies, KeffK_{\text{eff}} is a measured average that depends on the inputs and the strategy’s configuration. We distinguish between calibrated KeffcalibratedK_{\text{eff}}^{\text{calibrated}} and measured KeffK_{\text{eff}}. KeffcalibratedK_{\text{eff}}^{\text{calibrated}} is based on the number of active experts for the calibration set (Huang et al., 2026). Our analysis uses measured KeffK_{\text{eff}}, which counts expert activations at test time during the quality evaluation. The two may diverge because any threshold only enforces the target value on the calibration set, but may transfer imperfectly across datasets and depends heavily on the modality split, as demonstrated in Section 4.3.3.

The bottleneck for MoE inference depends on the deployment regime. At sufficiently large batch sizes, the expert feed-forward evaluation becomes compute-bound. In this case reducing the number of FLOPs provides the largest inference speed-up. The FLOPs of the expert matmuls scale linearly with the number of active experts per token: KeffK_{\text{eff}} is thus directly proportional to expert compute. Reducing active experts also lowers secondary costs such as all-to-all communication as described by Yang et al. (2025b). KeffK_{\text{eff}} counts only expert activations, ignoring other factors like routing, load imbalance, and communication overhead. This makes it a hardware-agnostic proxy for runtime cost, with true cost larger than what KeffK_{\text{eff}} implies. Figure 1 shows the monotonic but sublinear relationship between KeffK_{\text{eff}} and core inference metrics; we discuss this relation in Appendix A.5.

4 Results

4.1 Implementation

Several of these methods provide incomplete or no code releases, so we reimplement them on a best-effort basis. Ada-K has no release at all, and we reproduce its PPO-trained classifier ourselves (Appendix A.4), referring to it as the Allocator throughout. NAEE and DiEP release code only for Mixtral, a coarse-grained model, so we extend both to the k=8k=8 regime. Where a method natively exposes only a single operating point, we sweep its free parameter: the quantiles from 0.10.1 to 0.90.9 for NAEE and DiEP, thresholds for MoDES in order to trace a full frontier. We reproduce reported operating points from each original paper to confirm our implementations are faithful (Appendix A.7).

4.2 Text-only Evaluation

We compare all strategies at matched KeffK_{\text{eff}} on Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025a) and Gemma4-26B-A4B (Gemma Team et al., 2026), two popular mid-sized MoE models with k=8k=8 active experts. While most methods report only a single operating point (i.e., a single KeffK_{\text{eff}}) at which they report performance, we sweep each method’s tunable parameters to trace a full quality–compute frontier, providing clearer evidence of each method’s benefit at any given compute level. We evaluate on the zero-shot multiple-choice benchmarks HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) and ARC-C (Clark et al., 2018), as well as 5-shot GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and zero-shot HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) as generative benchmarks. A full overview of the benchmarks and corresponding calibration sets is given in Table 4. We use lm-eval (Gao et al., 2024) for consistency with related literature. KeffK_{\text{eff}} is measured at test time during each evaluation (Section 3.3); for GSM8K and HumanEval this includes the autoregressive decoding passes. Since most methods require calibration, we define a realistic calibration dataset, consisting of a mixed corpus of English, Chinese, code, and math built from C4_en and C4_zh (Raffel et al., 2023), open-web-math (Paster et al., 2023), and python-codes-25k (flytech, 2023). This realistic regime simulates the calibration–evaluation mismatch typical of actual deployments. We also evaluate the impact of calibration by evaluating a “best-case” scenario on the benchmarks’ own train sets.

4.2.1 Strategy comparison

Figure 2 shows the difference in performance between the strategies introduced in Table 1. The plot compares the mean relative performance drop across ARC-C, HellaSwag, HumanEval and GSM8K for different KeffK_{\text{eff}}. The Pareto frontier reveals a number of behaviors: first, NAEE most closely matches the fixed top-kk baseline for most points along the frontier, with some minor improvements compared to the baseline. The Allocator also shows some improvements in the KeffK_{\text{eff}} ≈1\approx 1 regime for Qwen3. However, overall benefit is very limited, at most ∼2.6\sim 2.6 pp compared to the interpolated baseline. This difference is especially small given the substantial quality loss already occurring in this KeffK_{\text{eff}} range: at this point the model has already lost 50% to 65% of its original capability. To provide context, at KeffK_{\text{eff}} ≤2.5\leq 2.5 the best strategy on Gemma4-26B-A4B performs worse on average than Gemma4-E4B, a dense model with 85%85\% fewer effective parameters11 1 Following the Gemma4 model card (Gemma Team et al., 2026), the count excludes embeddings; the 26B designation of the MoE follows the same convention.. This limits practical use of the observed gains. Both MoDES and DiEP mostly perform worse than the baseline, with MoDES only slightly ahead above KeffK_{\text{eff}} =1=1. MoDES does, however, achieve operating points below KeffK_{\text{eff}} =1=1, meaning that for some tokens the MoE block is completely skipped, a regime that the baseline cannot reach.

The composition of the drops also matters: as Figure 3 shows, the multiple-choice benchmarks degrade smoothly toward their random-guessing floors, while GSM8K collapses sharply once KeffK_{\text{eff}} falls below a model-dependent threshold (∼2{\sim}2 for Qwen3). HumanEval follows a similar pattern. Aggregate drops at low KeffK_{\text{eff}} are therefore dominated by generative-task failure, and the safe operating point is set by the generative benchmark for each model, not the average. Detailed per-benchmark results for Gemma4 are included in Appendix A.6.

To validate that this is not an artifact of our realistic calibration, we also evaluate a best-case scenario using the benchmarks’ own trainset. Figure 4 highlights the shift of the middle operating point when using best-case calibration. For DiEP and MoDES a substantial shift in KeffK_{\text{eff}} can be observed and both DiEP and the Allocator gain substantially compared to the realistic calibration. However, this gain does not enable the methods to outperform the static baseline. We provide further details in Appendix A.3.

4.3 Multimodal Evaluation

4.3.1 Setup

In the multimodal setting, we compare NAEE and MoDES against the static softmax top-kk baseline and our per-modality variant. The per-modality variant is motivated by prior observations that vision tokens tolerate substantially fewer experts than text tokens (Xia et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). DiEP, which underperformed the baseline in both text regimes, is excluded. The Ada-K Allocator is excluded as well. This is due to its loss formulation: the Allocator uses next-token prediction as its quality measure. Due to the training procedure of vision-language models, the per-token loss of vision tokens is never used during training, so they do not provide a quality signal that the Allocator could leverage. Applying the Allocator to multi-modal evaluations requires the implementation of a new loss formulation. As MoDES is natively designed for multimodal models, we expect it to perform best in this scenario. We use Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a), closely related to the Qwen3 model used in our text-only evaluation. To provide ideal conditions for MoDES, we calibrate it using its published GQA (Hudson & Manning, 2019) protocol; for consistency, we also calibrate NAEE on GQA. We evaluate on ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019), and MME (Fu et al., 2025), as well as DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021b), InfoVQA (Mathew et al., 2021a), and OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024) for text-heavy images. As in the text-only setting, we measure expert activations during evaluation to obtain KeffK_{\text{eff}}, computed over all routed tokens regardless of modality; we report the per-benchmark modality mix in Appendix A.2. Evaluation uses LMMS-Eval (Li et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024).

4.3.2 Multimodal Results

Figure 5 shows the relative drop compared to the full model across all six benchmarks, highlighting the performance differences across strategies. MoDES, which is modality-aware, outperforms NAEE as well as softmax top-kk by a large margin. However, it fails to outperform the per-modality softmax top-kk baseline. Again, MoDES finds KeffK_{\text{eff}} <1<1, which is not reachable by the baseline except when skipping the experts for vision tokens completely.

The only outlier is MME-Cognition, a sub-task of MME, (Figure 9, Appendix), where MoDES consistently leads the other approaches. The per-modality softmax strategy provides two recommended trade-off points: for ktext=8k_{\text{text}}=8, reducing kvisionk_{\text{vision}} to 1 incurs a drop of approximately 4.1%4.1\%, while reducing kvisionk_{\text{vision}} to 2 incurs an average drop of less than 1.8%1.8\%. Reducing kvisionk_{\text{vision}} to 1 reduces the number of active experts during the benchmark by ≈85%\approx 85\%, to a measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} of 1.08 on average. Reducing kvisionk_{\text{vision}} to zero increases the drop to 19.1%19.1\%. Surprisingly, this means that more than 80%80\% of quality is retained even though the vision tokens skip the experts entirely. Reducing ktextk_{\text{text}} to six allows further optimization of the number of active experts, while incurring a small quality drop compared to ktext=8k_{\text{text}}=8. The benefit of modality-awareness is direct: reducing experts to one for both modalities (softmax top-kk) costs more than 30%30\% of overall performance, while even the more extreme kvision=0k_{\text{vision}}=0 with text untouched (per-modality softmax top-kk) costs only 19.1%19.1\%.

Figure 6 decomposes the measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} by modality, showing how each strategy distributes its expert budget. Softmax top-kk and NAEE remain close to the symmetric diagonal, with NAEE allocating slightly more experts to vision tokens than to text tokens. This is the opposite of what the quality results favor. In contrast, MoDES retains nearly the full expert count for text tokens and concentrates skipping on vision tokens, closely following the per-modality baseline with ktext=8k_{\text{text}}=8. This is in line with the quality–compute frontiers, highlighting similar performance for similar skip patterns.

MoDES does provide a benefit in the sub-one expert regime. Without a finer (e.g. per-layer) granularity, our per-modality approach can only reduce KeffK_{\text{eff}} below 11 by setting kvision=0k_{\text{vision}}=0, which degrades performance to the point of limited practical use.

4.3.3 Calibrated and measured KeffK_{\text{eff}}

The deviation between calibrated and measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} is also substantial in these benchmarks; Table 2 quantifies this gap for the MoDES results. This deviation stems from two main factors: the modality split and routing scores. Depending on the actual workload, sequences may have a different share of image vs. text tokens. Since more experts are skipped for image tokens, a lower proportion of image tokens shifts KeffK_{\text{eff}} upward, and vice versa. A second factor is differences in routing scores. Since MoDES uses the routing scores for skipping, different routing score distributions in the evaluation data may also influence how many experts are actually skipped. Both factors introduce a degree of unpredictability: the actual average number of remaining active experts can deviate from the calibrated figure by more than 50%, even on benchmarks from the same task family as the calibration set (short-answer VQA; cf. Appendix A.2).

When evaluating on a text-only benchmark, in this case GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), the pattern is amplified. Text-only prompts are a typical use case for vision-enabled models, since many modern models bundle multimodal support into an otherwise general-purpose base model. Table 2 shows that for GSM8K, the KeffK_{\text{eff}} for MoDES shifts to 7.96, far from the KeffcalibratedK_{\text{eff}}^{\text{calibrated}} 1.2: the calibrated skipping effectively deactivates, and MoDES retains quality only by reverting to nearly the full model: the calibrated compute saving vanishes. Our per-modality baseline also shifts with the workload, but is bounded by construction at KeffK_{\text{eff}} =ktext=6=k_{\text{text}}=6, where it lands exactly, trading 2.7 pp of accuracy (68.8% vs. 71.5%) for 25% fewer active experts than MoDES actually uses.

5 Discussion

While the trained or calibrated methods such as NAEE and the Allocator (Ada-K) can provide quality benefits compared to the baseline in some cases, these are in our experiments limited to 2.62.6 pp, often also in regimes where quality has already degraded substantially. Furthermore, the high dependence on calibration data suggests that any minor performance benefit from one of the calibrated strategies comes at the cost of performance in another area or domain. Beyond the standard calibration, identifying operating points and hyperparameters is a challenge, especially for RL-based Ada-K (Eimer et al., 2023).

The multimodal results support the same overall conclusions: MoDES outperforms both NAEE and the modality-unaware static baseline, showing that modality is valuable for deciding whether to skip experts for a given token. However, MoDES’s advantage over a calibration-free modality-aware baseline is confined to the sub-one KeffK_{\text{eff}} regime; for larger KeffK_{\text{eff}} the static baseline matches or outperforms it. We conclude that calibrated thresholds provide a benefit beyond treating vision and text tokens independently only in this sub-one KeffK_{\text{eff}} regime, but at the cost of complexity with only a modest runtime improvement as shown in Appendix A.5.

Beyond the one-time calibration effort, matching strategies at equal KeffK_{\text{eff}} also understates the true runtime cost. Every dynamic method adds a routing decision to each forward pass. Dynamic skipping also forfeits the uniform per-token compute of static top-kk, and with it the load balancing and latency guarantees quantified in Appendix A.5. Both effects are excluded from our KeffK_{\text{eff}}-matched analysis, which therefore favors the adaptive strategies. Finally, the calibrated methods offer no guarantee on the realized KeffK_{\text{eff}}: as Table 2 shows, measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} can deviate substantially from the calibrated target.

Practical Recommendation

The added benefit of the dynamic skipping methods rarely outweighs the required calibration overhead and complexity. For a practical multimodal inference scenario, statically reducing kvisionk_{\text{vision}} to 1–2 and ktextk_{\text{text}} to 6 for a model with eight active experts provides a strong trade-off between quality (<5%<5\% drop) and inference speed-up. For text-only models, the approach is similar: reducing kk to 6 provides a measurable inference speed-up with only a minor quality loss. Going beyond this point becomes heavily model-dependent and should be validated with a generative benchmark, as models tend to perform differently at those points.

To verify that this recommendation is not an artifact of the benchmarks used for its selection, we apply the operating point unchanged to MVBench (Li et al., 2024b), a held-out video benchmark. With kvision=1k_{\text{vision}}=1 and ktext=6k_{\text{text}}=6, the model achieves an accuracy of 69.9569.95 versus 71.4071.40 for the full model, a relative drop of 2.0%2.0\% at a measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} of 1.19. As video sequences are dominated by vision tokens, this represents an 85%85\% reduction in active experts. This minimal quality loss, on a workload and modality mix entirely outside the data used for calibration or selection, demonstrates the transferability of our recommendation. We also evaluate a larger model, GLM-4.6V (GLM-V Team et al., 2025), where the same operating point incurs an average drop of 4.2% (Appendix A.8).

Method design

Our results further highlight a significant gap in existing research: across compared methods as well as concurrent work such as ACE (Xu et al., 2026) comparisons lack a consistent static-kk control at matched measured compute and modality. When controlling for both, methods fail to consistently outperform the baseline. We therefore recommend that every future method compares against a static control at matched (measured) KeffK_{\text{eff}} that also uses any structural signal (e.g. modality) the method exploits.

6 Conclusion

Across three models as well as two held-out checks, none of the calibrated or learned skipping methods consistently outperform a static reduction of kk at matched measured KeffK_{\text{eff}}. The methods add calibration and tuning overhead and their realized KeffK_{\text{eff}} can deviate from the calibrated target (≥6×\geq 6\times in our experiments). This holds for text-only and multimodal models alike. We recommend static per-modality kk as the default, and a static control at matched measured KeffK_{\text{eff}} as the baseline for future methods.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for implementing methods (including general coding assistance) and providing feedback on research methodology. We have not used generative AI tools for proposing or refining hypotheses, interpreting results, or developing theoretical models or conceptual frameworks. Generating synthetic datasets, formulating mathematical claims, providing critical ingredients for proving mathematical claims, writing proofs, translation, cleaning and reformatting datasets, and qualitative or thematic data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for literature research, brainstorming and editing for readability. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. All LLM-generated code was reviewed by the authors and validated against existing results from literature. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

A.3 Calibration Sensitivity

All considered methods except the static baselines require calibration data. To establish the impact of the calibration data choice, we compare two regimes on ARC-C and HellaSwag: best-case, calibrated on the benchmark’s own train split, and realistic, calibrated on a mixed corpus of English, Chinese, code, and math built from C4_en and C4_zh (Raffel et al., 2023), open-web-math (Paster et al., 2023), and python-codes-25k (flytech, 2023). The realistic regime simulates the calibration–evaluation mismatch typical of actual deployments, while the best-case regime represents the most favorable calibration setting.

Figure 7 highlights the impact of the calibration data. We select the middle point of the corresponding threshold sweep and observe the change in quality between best-case and realistic calibration. In some cases this best-case calibration does provide benefits compared to the realistic calibration. However, these improvements are marginal and do not materially affect the performance relative to the baseline. Further, we observe that the change in calibration set leads to substantial shifts in KeffK_{\text{eff}} at identical thresholds. NAEE, the best-performing dynamic skipping method in the practically relevant regime, is also the most robust to the choice of calibration data, showing only minimal shifts under best-case calibration. Preliminary experiments highlighted this as well: even a mismatched calibration set (MATH only) led to very similar performance.

A.5 Runtime Performance

To validate KeffK_{\text{eff}} as a proxy for inference performance, we measure end-to-end inference with statically constrained expert counts using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). This constitutes an upper bound on the gains achievable by any strategy at a given KeffK_{\text{eff}}, as it excludes both routing-decision overhead and raggedness in per-token expert allocation; the static top-kk baseline attains this bound by construction. Standardized evaluation uses GuideLLM (Neural Magic, Inc., 2024) to benchmark Qwen3-30B-A3B on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, in two scenarios: synchronous (batch size 1, memory-bandwidth bound) and throughput (batch size 256, compute bound). We use GuideLLM’s ‘chat’ scenario to generate prompts. Figure 1 reports time-to-first-token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and output throughput. Reducing KeffK_{\text{eff}} from 8 to 1 lowers TTFT and ITL by 18% in the synchronous scenario and lowers TTFT by ∼30%\sim 30\% and ITL by ∼25%\sim 25\% in the throughput scenario, while output throughput rises from 111 to 135 tokens/s (1.22×1.22\times) and from ∼1.9\sim 1.9k to ∼2.65\sim 2.65k tokens/s (1.39×1.39\times), respectively. Notably, these gains are far below the 8×8\times reduction in expert compute: even under ideal static skipping, the end-to-end benefit is bounded well below proportionality, further compressing the value of the marginal quality differences between skipping strategies. The MoE blocks of the model only make up part of the overhead incurred; components such as attention, KV-Cache traffic, and non-expert weights are not addressed by any skipping technique and still incur computational costs.

A.6 Detailed Benchmark Results

To highlight the differences in performance we provide the detailed per-benchmark sweep results in Figures 8 and 9. A number of differences can be observed in both the text and multimodal context.

Text-only

In the text-only results, the performance characteristics for our generative benchmark and the multiple-choice benchmarks differ. ARC-C and HellaSwag performance decays smoothly towards the random selection floor, with all methods performing reasonably close to one another. For GSM8K this changes dramatically: for both models, the drop towards zero score is apparent and linked to dropping the number of experts beyond a certain point. Especially for Gemma4, no strategy is able to retain reasonable performance once fewer than 3 experts remain active, and some strategies already fail at 4. This is likely a combination of factors: first, we use strict-match for evaluation. This means that the model will score 0 when it fails to match the correct output format. Second, MoDES in particular can reduce the number of experts to 0 for some tokens, potentially breaking causal generation or reasoning. HumanEval performs similar to GSM8K.

Multimodal

For multimodal evaluation the performance varies less across benchmarks with a notable exception. The MME perception score shows limited drop even when vision tokens receive zero experts, provided enough experts are allocated to the text tokens. This differs from the MME cognition score, where the drop is more apparent and MoDES markedly outperforms the baseline rather than simply matching it.

A.7 Validating Implementations

Due to the incomplete nature of some of the code releases, we validate each method in the setting reported by its original authors.

NAEE

The NAEE code release only contains implementations for Mixtral 8x7B. To validate our implementation, we aim to reproduce their domain-specific calibration and evaluation regime. We calibrate Mixtral 8x7B (Jiang et al., 2024) on the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) and evaluate performance on 5-shot GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) using strict-match accuracy. We use NAEE’s default q=0.5q=0.5 quantile (median) skip criterion, as described in their methodology. The reported accuracy from the NAEE paper is 54.2854.28 (Lu et al., 2024), which corresponds to a 7.4%7.4\% relative drop compared to the original 58.6158.61. Our reimplementation achieved a baseline score of 58.5258.52 and an expert skipping score of 55.4255.42 (a 5.3% relative drop). This minor difference could be attributable to a number of factors, including slight differences between the cumulative-rule from the appendix and the two expert rule they describe in the paper. However, as the scores are very close, we are confident our implementation does not disadvantage NAEE in the comparison.

DiEP

Validation on DiEP was conducted on Mixtral 8x7B, evaluating the average accuracy across MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), and RTE (Dagan et al., 2005). Calibration was done on the “mixed” set, as it has significant overlap with the original C4 (Raffel et al., 2023) calibration data used in the DiEP paper (Bai et al., 2025b). Since the complete skip configuration is not explicitly reported, we again use the q=0.5q=0.5 quantile calibration that serves as their operating point elsewhere in the paper. Bai et al. (2025b) report an average accuracy of 65.165.1 for the base model and 64.164.1 after skipping, a 1.6%1.6\% relative drop; per-task scores are reported for the base model only. As Table 6 shows, our measured baseline matches theirs on every task when OpenBookQA is scored with unnormalized accuracy (65.665.6 vs. 65.165.1 on average); the apparent baseline gap under our default reporting (68.668.6) stems entirely from using length-normalized accuracy on OpenBookQA (49.049.0 vs. 37.237.2 unnormalized). Our reimplementation, which includes the from-scratch CKA computation absent from the public release, yields a relative drop of 2.6%2.6\% in DiEP’s metric convention (65.6→64.065.6\rightarrow 64.0; 2.1%2.1\% with length-normalized OpenBookQA). The difference to the reported 1.6%1.6\% is dominated by RTE (71.5→67.571.5\rightarrow 67.5), the smallest of the four tasks (277277 test examples, standard error ≈2.7\approx 2.7 pp), and is therefore within evaluation noise; the remaining tasks degrade by at most 1.41.4 points. We conclude that our implementation reproduces the reported behavior closely.

MoDES

For multimodal MoDES we use the original calibration method included with their code release. As we reimplement the routing function, we validate it by comparing our results against the reported values for TextVQA in Table 7. We use the same routing function for the text-only evaluation, but deviate from the original calibration: we calibrate on the text datasets and conduct a sweep across thresholds rather than using the frontier search described in the paper. Since the text-only evaluation uses the identical routing function, validated above, and differs only in the calibration procedure, we treat it as a faithful application of the method rather than a separate reproduction.

Ada-K

No public implementation or model checkpoints were available for Ada-K as of writing. As such, we reproduced its classifier architecture ourselves, which we refer to throughout as the Allocator. We train it using the same PPO approach as the original Ada-K paper. Some variance is nonetheless expected, due to the nature of reinforcement learning: its sensitivity to hyper-parameters (Eimer et al., 2023) is itself part of the practical complexity we discuss in Section 5. To validate the performance of our Allocator, we ran Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, trained the Allocator on our mixed dataset, and evaluated on 25-shot ARC-C. Our Allocator achieved a score of 53.9253.92 at KeffK_{\text{eff}} =2.45=2.45, very close to the reported 54.4154.41 at a slightly higher KeffK_{\text{eff}} =2.58=2.58, consistent with the slightly larger expert budget.

A.8 Scaling to larger models

We also evaluate our recommendation on another (larger) model: GLM-4.6V (GLM-V Team et al., 2025). It natively has k=8k=8 and 128 available experts. It also has a shared expert, differentiating it from Qwen3-VL. We evaluate the operating point ktext=6k_{\text{text}}=6 and kvision=1k_{\text{vision}}=1 and observe an average drop of 4.2% compared to the original model across ChartQA, TextVQA and MME. Full results are included in Table 8. As can be seen the drop is dominated by MME-Cognition.
